indiaMissions/india-women-ramabai/title: Women's missions, Pandita Ramabai and the Mukti revival
indiaMissions/india-women-ramabai/summar: From the 1830s women's missionary societies sent single women to teach in girls' schools and visit secluded high-caste women in their homes (zenana work), and by 1900 women formed the majority of the Protestant missionary force. The most remarkable figure of this world was an Indian convert, the Sanskrit scholar Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922), whose homes for widows and famine orphans at Pune and Kedgaon became the Mukti Mission and the setting of the 1905 Mukti revival, an early source of Indian Pentecostalism.
indiaMissions/india-women-ramabai/story:
Missionary education for Indian girls began in the shadow of the men's missions: Hannah Marshman opened schools at Serampore in the early 1800s and Mary Ann Cooke (later Wilson) started girls' schools in Calcutta in 1822. The Society for Promoting Female Education in the East (1834) and the Indian Female Normal School Society (1852, later the Zenana Bible and Medical Mission) sent women teachers, and in Calcutta Hannah Catherine Mullens pioneered ‘zenana visiting’ in the 1850s, teaching reading and needlework — and the Bible — to secluded upper-caste women whom male missionaries could not meet. American women organised their own boards: the interdenominational Woman's Union Missionary Society (1861) and the Methodist Woman's Foreign Missionary Society (1869), which in 1870 sent Isabella Thoburn to Lucknow and the physician Clara Swain to Bareilly. The Church of England Zenana Missionary Society followed in 1880. By the end of the century women missionaries outnumbered men in most Protestant missions, and girls' schools, women's colleges and women's hospitals formed a large share of mission work.

Isabella Thoburn opened a school for six girls in a rented room in the Lucknow bazaar in 1870; it became the Lal Bagh school and, from 1886, the college that bears her name, one of the first Christian colleges for women in Asia. Its graduates and teachers included Lilavati Singh, who represented Indian women at international missionary gatherings. Indian Christian women became writers and reformers in their own right: Krupabai Satthianadhan wrote the first novels in English by an Indian woman (‘Kamala’ and ‘Saguna’, 1890s), Ellen Lakshmi Goreh wrote hymns, and the Sorabji sisters founded schools in Pune and, in Cornelia Sorabji's case, became India's first woman lawyer.

Pandita Ramabai was born Ramabai Dongre in 1858 into a Chitpavan Brahmin family; her father, unusually, taught his wife and daughter Sanskrit. After her parents and sister died in the famine of 1874–77 she and her brother wandered as reciters of the Puranas, and in Calcutta in 1878 the pandits gave her the titles ‘Pandita’ and ‘Sarasvati’. She married a Bengali lawyer of lower caste, Bipin Behari Medhvi, was widowed in 1882 with an infant daughter, Manorama, and moved to Pune, where she founded the Arya Mahila Samaj and gave evidence to the Hunter Education Commission. In 1883 she went to England with the help of the Anglican Community of St Mary the Virgin at Wantage, where she was baptised; but she resisted the sisters' attempts to make her an orthodox Anglican, insisting on her own reading of scripture and her Indian identity. In the United States (1886–88) she published ‘The High-Caste Hindu Woman’ (1887), a powerful indictment of child marriage and the treatment of widows, and organised Ramabai Associations to fund a school for widows.

Her Sharada Sadan (Home of Learning) opened in Bombay on 11 March 1889 and moved to Pune in 1890, run on officially non-sectarian lines with support from Hindu reformers. When several widows chose baptism, the nationalist press led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak's ‘Kesari’ accused her of proselytising under false pretences, and in 1893 most Hindu members of the advisory committee resigned and many pupils were withdrawn. After an evangelical conversion experience in 1891 Ramabai moved towards open evangelism. During the famine of 1896–97 she travelled into the Central Provinces and brought back several hundred destitute girls and women, and later others from the Gujarat famine of 1900; she built Mukti Sadan (House of Salvation) on land at Kedgaon, east of Pune, together with Kripa Sadan for ‘fallen’ women and homes for the blind. By 1900 about 1,500 women and girls lived at Mukti, with farms, a printing press, weaving and other industries.

From January 1905, after Ramabai had heard of the Welsh and Khasi revivals, prayer circles of hundreds of Mukti girls met daily; on 29–30 June 1905 a revival broke out marked by confession of sin, weeping, visions, ecstatic prayer and, by late 1906, speaking in tongues. Bands of young women went out to preach in surrounding villages. The American Methodist Minnie Abrams, Ramabai's co-worker, described it in ‘The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire’ (1906), which circulated in the United States and Chile, and the Mukti revival became one of the earliest sources of Pentecostalism independent of Azusa Street. Ramabai herself remained cautious about tongues as a necessary sign.

In her last decades Ramabai learned Greek and Hebrew and translated the whole Bible into simple Marathi, finishing the proofs shortly before her death on 5 April 1922; Manorama had died the previous year. The British government awarded her the Kaiser-i-Hind medal in 1919, and India issued a postage stamp in her honour in 1989. Feminist historians now see her as one of the foremost Indian social reformers of the nineteenth century, while evangelicals remember her as a revivalist and Bible translator; she herself refused to fit either the Brahmin reformist or the Western missionary mould. The Mukti Mission continues at Kedgaon, caring for women and children.

indiaMissions/india-women-ramabai/focus/: Female literacy and schooling at a time when only about 0.6% of Indian women could read (Census 1901).
Shelter, education and vocational training for widows and orphans.
Campaigns against child marriage, enforced widowhood and the seclusion of women.
Bible teaching and conversion, increasingly explicit at Mukti after 1891.

indiaMissions/india-women-ramabai/strate: Separate women's missionary boards and single women missionaries, funded largely by women's donations in Britain and North America.
Zenana visiting: teaching reading and handicrafts in the women's quarters as a door to Bible teaching.
Boarding schools and colleges for girls (Isabella Thoburn College, Sarah Tucker College at Palayamkottai, Women's Christian College Madras).
Ramabai's institution-building: self-supporting farms, a printing press, weaving and dairying at Mukti to make residents independent.
Indian women's leadership — Bible women, teachers and evangelistic bands rather than reliance on foreign staff.
Use of international networks (Ramabai Associations in the USA, holiness and revival periodicals) for funding and publicity.
indiaMissions/india-women-ramabai/challe: Hindu reformers and nationalists accused Sharada Sadan of breaking its non-sectarian promise; the 1893 resignations and withdrawals nearly wrecked it.
Ramabai's independence troubled Anglican mentors, who disliked her doctrinal views, and some missionaries who disliked an Indian woman directing a large institution.
Famine, plague (1897–1902) and disease among the destitute children who came to Mukti.
Social barriers: purdah, early marriage and opposition from families to girls' schooling.
Financial dependence on foreign donors, especially after Hindu support collapsed.
Controversy over the emotional manifestations of the 1905 revival.
indiaMissions/india-women-ramabai/harms/: Zenana work was openly designed as an evangelistic wedge into Hindu and Muslim homes, which fed suspicion of all female education as covert proselytism.
Missionary fundraising literature often portrayed Indian women as degraded victims of ‘heathenism’, reinforcing Western stereotypes and colonial justifications.
Mission schools frequently required Bible instruction and pressed pupils towards baptism, separating some converts from their families.
Institutional life at Mukti was strict and paternalistic, and orphans had little choice about their religious upbringing.
Western women missionaries sometimes treated Indian Christian women as subordinates rather than colleagues, a pattern Ramabai herself resisted.
indiaMissions/india-women-ramabai/outcom: A network of girls' schools and women's colleges that produced many of India's first women graduates, teachers, doctors and nurses.
Ramabai's writings and testimony shaped public debate on widow remarriage, the age of consent and women's education.
The Mukti revival (1905–07) helped give rise to Indian and Chilean Pentecostalism and influenced revival movements worldwide.
A complete Marathi Bible translated from the original languages by an Indian woman (published 1924).
The Mukti Mission continues at Kedgaon as a home and school for women and children.
A model of Indian Christian leadership by a woman, widely cited in Indian feminist and church history.

indiaMissions/india-women-ramabai/legacy: Women's missions turned female education from a curiosity into an expectation in many Indian communities and gave Indian Christian women public roles decades before most of their contemporaries. Pandita Ramabai stands at the centre of that story: a Brahmin scholar who became a Christian without becoming a Westerner, a reformer whose critique of caste and patriarchy was sharpened by her faith, and the leader of a revival that fed the global Pentecostal movement. Her life also shows the costs of conversion in colonial India, where every school and shelter was read as part of a struggle over religion and nation.
